opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it really came down to who we thought the customer was going to be. When we started Parallel, our view was that the primary user of the web was going to shift from humans to AIs, and agents just have a very different set of needs than a person typing into a search box.

For a human, latency is everything. If a results page takes three seconds to load, you've lost them. But an agent doing real work, say researching a market, filling out a due diligence checklist, or enriching thousands of records, cares much more about whether the information it gets back is correct and complete. A wrong or shallow answer that comes back fast is actually worse than useless, because the agent builds on it and the error compounds through the rest of the task.

So quality was the first thing. We wanted to be able to say with confidence that on the hard, multi-hop, long-tail questions, we were giving agents the best information available. That's the part that's genuinely difficult to build, and it's where we felt the existing tools, which were designed for human attention spans, were leaving the most value on the table.

Cost was the second thing because agents consume the web at a completely different scale. A person might do a handful of searches; an agent might do hundreds or thousands in a single workflow. If each one is expensive, the economics of the whole application break. So we wanted developers to be able to dial how much compute they spend per query and get a predictable price-to-quality tradeoff.

Latency we treated as something we could engineer down over time. It's very hard to bolt quality onto a fast but shallow system after the fact. It's much more tractable to take a system that gets the right answer and make it faster. So the sequencing was deliberate: get the hard thing right first, make it affordable, and then compress the time. And we've been doing that, offering faster tiers as use cases like real-time chat started needing them, without giving up the accuracy that made the product worth using in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says latency was something they could engineer down over time and was more tractable to improve after building a system with the right answers, while describing quality as the difficult part.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we started Parallel, the thing we kept coming back to was that we were building for agents, not for people typing into a box. And that changes the whole set of tradeoffs.

If you think about classic web search, latency is king. A person is sitting there waiting, and a few hundred milliseconds matters enormously to whether they come back. The whole stack at Google and at Twitter was optimized around that. But an AI agent doing research isn't sitting there drumming its fingers. It's in the middle of a long task. It might make dozens or hundreds of calls to the web to answer one question. What it cares about is: did I get the right information, and can I afford to do this at scale?

So we made a deliberate bet. First, quality. If a model is going to reason over what you return, a wrong or shallow result doesn't just cost you a click, it compounds. The agent builds on it, and now the whole downstream chain is wrong. So we spent a lot of effort on actually understanding the task, going deeper on pages, returning the content the model needs rather than ten blue links.

Second, cost. When you move from one query per human intention to hundreds of queries per agent task, the economics are totally different. If every call is expensive, nobody can build anything real on top of you. So we had to design the system so that doing a lot of web research is cheap enough to be the default behavior, not a luxury.

Latency was always on the roadmap, and we've worked on it a lot since. But the sequencing mattered. If we'd optimized for speed first, we'd have been building a slightly better version of the old thing for a user that doesn't exist anymore. We wanted to get right what agents actually need, and then make it fast. I think if you get the first two right, you earn the chance to work on the third.

r001.rationale: The response says agents tolerate latency and that Parallel prioritized quality and cost first, but it does not explain that latency reduction was deferred because it was established engineering rather than uncertain research.

astra-6.text:
Early on, we wanted to establish that we could deliver useful search results at a cost that made sense. If the results weren’t good enough, making them faster wouldn’t solve the core problem. And if they were too expensive, people couldn’t use them at the scale we envisioned.

Latency still mattered, but we saw it as a tradeoff we could optimize once we understood the quality and cost requirements. That was the sequencing: first make the search useful and economical, then make it faster.

r001.rationale: The response says latency could be optimized later, after establishing quality and cost, but does not explain that latency reduction was established engineering rather than uncertain research.

sol-6.1.text:
We were building search for AI agents, so the tradeoffs were different from search for a person. A person sitting in front of a search box really notices latency. An agent might be doing research in the background, and what matters more is whether it gets the right information and how much it costs to complete the task.

So we initially focused on quality and cost because those determined whether the product was useful at all. If you return the wrong information quickly, you haven’t helped. And if an agent needs to make many searches, cost becomes a real constraint. Latency still matters, but we wanted to establish that foundation first.

r001.rationale: The response says latency mattered less for background agent research and prioritized quality and cost, but does not say latency reduction was established engineering rather than uncertain research.
